amc12-2015-12a-02.title: Triangle inequality
amc12-2015-12a-02.body:
The third side $x$ satisfies $20-15<x<20+15$, i.e. $5<x<35$. So the perimeter $35+x$ is strictly between $40$ and $70$. Only $72$ is outside this range.

**Answer: (E) 72**

amc12-2015-12a-02.title: Test the largest choice
amc12-2015-12a-02.body:
A perimeter of $72$ would need a third side of $37$, but $15+20=35<37$, so such a triangle can't close up. The other choices need third sides $17,22,27,32$, all between $5$ and $35$.

**Answer: (E) 72**

amc12-2015-12a-05.title: Think about each part
amc12-2015-12a-05.body:
To make $\frac ab-c$ bigger we want $\frac ab$ bigger and $c$ smaller. A fraction gets bigger when the numerator goes up and the denominator goes down. So round $a$ up, $b$ down, and $c$ down: that guarantees a larger result.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-2015-12a-05.title: Counterexamples for the others
amc12-2015-12a-05.body:
In (A), (B), (C), (E) at least one change pushes the result down, and it can outweigh the others. For example in (A), with $a=100$, $b=10$, $c=10$ (exact value $0$), rounding to $a=100$, $b=20$, $c=20$ gives $-15$. Similar examples work for (B), (C), (E). In (D) all three changes push the result up.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-2015-12a-09.title: Symmetry
amc12-2015-12a-09.body:
The order in which the girls pick doesn't matter: Cheryl's two marbles are just a random pair out of the six. There are $\binom62=15$ pairs, and $3$ of them are same-coloured. Probability $\frac3{15}=\frac15$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac15$**

amc12-2015-12a-09.title: Count arrangements
amc12-2015-12a-09.body:
Line the six marbles up in a random order; Carol gets positions 1–2, Claudia 3–4, Cheryl 5–6. Whatever marble is in position 5, the marble in position 6 is one of the remaining 5, and exactly 1 of them matches. Probability $\frac15$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac15$**

amc12-2015-12a-10.title: Simon's favourite factoring trick
amc12-2015-12a-10.body:
Add 1: $xy+x+y+1=81$, so $(x+1)(y+1)=81$. With $x>y>0$, both factors are at least 2 and $x+1>y+1$: the only option is $27\cdot3$. So $x=26$, $y=2$.

**Answer: (E) 26**

amc12-2015-12a-11.title: Go through the positions
amc12-2015-12a-11.body:
Let $d$ be the distance between the centres.

- $d<1$ (one circle inside the other, including concentric): $0$ lines.
- $d=1$ (internally tangent): $1$ line.
- $1<d<5$ (two intersection points): $2$ lines.
- $d=5$ (externally tangent): $3$ lines.
- $d>5$ (separate): $4$ lines.

The radii differ, so the circles never coincide. That gives $k\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$: 5 values.

**Answer: (D) 5**

amc12-2015-12a-11.title: External and internal tangents
amc12-2015-12a-11.body:
Common tangents come in two kinds: external ones (both circles on the same side) and internal ones (circles on opposite sides). External tangents exist (two of them) unless one circle is inside the other; they merge into one when the circles are internally tangent. Internal tangents exist only when the circles don't overlap: two if separate, one if externally tangent. Combining: $0,1,2,3,4$ — five possibilities.

**Answer: (D) 5**

amc12-2015-12a-12.title: Find the kite
amc12-2015-12a-12.body:
The $y$-intercepts are $(0,-2)$ and $(0,4)$. The $x$-intercepts are $\pm\sqrt{2/a}$ and $\pm\sqrt{4/b}$; for there to be only four points in total they must coincide: $\frac2a=\frac4b$.

The kite has diagonals $6$ (vertical) and $2\sqrt{2/a}$ (horizontal), so its area is $\frac12\cdot6\cdot2\sqrt{2/a}=6\sqrt{2/a}=12$. Thus $\sqrt{2/a}=2$, $a=\frac12$, and $b=2a=1$. So $a+b=1.5$.

**Answer: (B) 1.5**

amc12-2015-12a-12.title: Work backwards from the area
amc12-2015-12a-12.body:
The vertical diagonal is from $-2$ to $4$, length $6$. Area $12$ forces the horizontal diagonal to be $\frac{2\cdot12}6=4$, so both parabolas cross the $x$-axis at $\pm2$. Then $0=4a-2$ gives $a=\frac12$ and $0=4-4b$ gives $b=1$.

**Answer: (B) 1.5**

amc12-2015-12a-13.title: Find a counterexample
amc12-2015-12a-13.body:
If every game is a draw, each team plays 11 games and scores $11$. Then the highest score is $11<12$, so (E) is false.

The others are true: every game gives out 2 points, and there are $\binom{12}2=66$ games, so the total is $132$ — even and at least $100$ (A, D). With an even number of odd scores among 12, the number of even scores is also even (B). Two teams can't both score 0, since their game against each other gives at least 1 point (C).

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-2015-12a-13.title: Average score
amc12-2015-12a-13.body:
The total is always $2\cdot66=132$, so the average is $11$. The highest score is at least the average, $11$, but need not be $12$: it is exactly $11$ when all teams score the same, as happens when all games are draws. So (E) is the false statement.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-2015-12a-14.title: Flip the logs
amc12-2015-12a-14.body:
$\frac1{\log_b a}=\log_a b$, so the equation is $\log_a2+\log_a3+\log_a4=\log_a24=1$. Hence $a=24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

amc12-2015-12a-14.title: Natural logs
amc12-2015-12a-14.body:
$\frac1{\log_b a}=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, so the equation says $\frac{\ln2+\ln3+\ln4}{\ln a}=1$, i.e. $\ln a=\ln 24$ and $a=24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

amc12-2015-12a-15.title: Make the denominator a power of 10
amc12-2015-12a-15.body:
$\frac{123456789}{2^{26}5^4}=\frac{123456789\cdot5^{22}}{10^{26}}$. The numerator is not divisible by $10$ (it is odd), so the last digit of the decimal is in the 26th place: 26 digits.

**Answer: (C) 26**

amc12-2015-12a-15.title: Repeatedly halve
amc12-2015-12a-15.body:
Dividing by $5^4$ and multiplying by $2^4$ is the same as dividing by $10^4$, so the value is $\frac{123456789}{2^{22}\cdot10^4}$. Dividing an odd number by $2$ adds one decimal place each time (it ends in 5), so dividing by $2^{22}$ gives exactly 22 decimal places, and shifting by $10^4$ adds 4 more: 26.

**Answer: (C) 26**

amc12-2015-12a-20.title: Set up and factor
amc12-2015-12a-20.body:
$T$ has perimeter $18$ and area $\frac12\cdot8\cdot3=12$. For $T'$: $2a+b=18$, so $a=9-\frac b2$, and the height is $\sqrt{a^2-\frac{b^2}4}=\sqrt{81-9b}$. Area: $\frac b2\sqrt{81-9b}=12$, so $b^2(81-9b)=576$, i.e. $b^2(9-b)=64$, or $b^3-9b^2+64=0$.

$b=8$ is a root (that's $T$ itself), so $(b-8)(b^2-b-8)=0$, and the other positive root is $b=\frac{1+\sqrt{33}}2\approx\frac{1+5.74}2\approx3.37$. Closest: $3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

amc12-2015-12a-20.title: Heron's formula
amc12-2015-12a-20.body:
With semiperimeter $9$, Heron gives area$^2=9(9-a)^2(9-b)$. For $T$ this is $9\cdot16\cdot1=144$. For $T'$, with $9-a=\frac b2$: $9\cdot\frac{b^2}4(9-b)=144$, i.e. $b^2(9-b)=64$. Try values: $b=3$: $54$; $b=3.5$: $67.4$; so the root is between 3 and 3.5 (about $3.37$), closest to $3$. The other root $b=8$ is $T$ itself.

**Answer: (A) 3**

amc12-2015-12a-21.title: Track the circle as its centre moves
amc12-2015-12a-21.body:
The ellipse is $\frac{x^2}{16}+y^2=1$ with foci $(\pm\sqrt{15},0)$. A circle through both foci has centre $(0,k)$ and $r^2=15+k^2$; by symmetry take $k\ge0$.

- The smallest such circle ($k=0$, $r=\sqrt{15}$) meets the ellipse in four points (solving gives $y^2=\frac1{15}$).
- As $k$ grows, the lowest point of the circle, $(0,k-r)$, moves down. Four intersection points remain until it reaches the ellipse's bottom vertex $(0,-1)$, where the circle becomes tangent there (only three points). That happens when $r=k+1$: $15+k^2=(k+1)^2$, so $k=7$ and $r=8$.
- For $r>8$ the circle only meets the ellipse at two points.

So $r\in[\sqrt{15},8)$ and $a+b=\sqrt{15}+8$.

**Answer: (D) $\sqrt{15}+8$**

amc12-2015-12a-21.title: Algebraic count
amc12-2015-12a-21.body:
Substitute $x^2=16-16y^2$ into the circle $x^2+y^2-2ky=15$: $16-15y^2-2ky=15$, i.e. $15y^2+2ky-1=0$. This always has one positive and one negative root $y$ (product $-\frac1{15}$). Each root with $|y|<1$ gives two points $(\pm x,y)$; $|y|=1$ gives one point. The positive root is always below $1$ for $k\ge0$; the negative root is $>-1$ exactly when $15-2k-1>0$, i.e. $k<7$. So four points iff $0\le k<7$, i.e. $\sqrt{15}\le r<8$, and $a+b=\sqrt{15}+8$.

**Answer: (D) $\sqrt{15}+8$**

amc12-2015-12a-22.title: Runs, a recursion, and residues mod 3 and mod 4
amc12-2015-12a-22.body:
A valid sequence is determined by its first letter ($2$ choices) and its list of run lengths, each $1$, $2$ or $3$, adding up to $n$. So $S(n)=2T(n)$, where $T(n)$ is the number of ways to write $n$ as an ordered sum of 1s, 2s and 3s. Looking at the last part, $T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+T(n-3)$ with $T(0)=1$, $T(1)=1$, $T(2)=2$.

$S(n)\bmod12$ is determined by $S(n)\bmod4$ and $S(n)\bmod3$, i.e. by $T(n)\bmod2$ and $T(n)\bmod3$. Since each term depends only on the previous three, the residues repeat as soon as three consecutive residues repeat.

- Mod 2: $T(n)$ runs $1,1,0,0,\;1,1,0,0,\dots$ (period 4). As $2015\equiv3\pmod4$, $T(2015)$ is even and $S(2015)\equiv0\pmod4$.
- Mod 3: $T(n)$ runs $1,1,2,1,1,1,0,2,0,2,1,0,0,\;1,1,2,\dots$ (period 13). As $2015=13\cdot155$, $T(2015)\equiv T(0)=1$ and $S(2015)\equiv2\pmod3$.

The residue mod 12 that is $\equiv0\pmod4$ and $\equiv2\pmod3$ is $8$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

amc12-2015-12a-24.title: When is the imaginary part zero?
amc12-2015-12a-24.body:
The allowed values are $0,1,\frac12,\frac32,\frac13,\frac23,\frac43,\frac53,\frac14,\frac34,\frac54,\frac74$ and the eight fractions $\frac k5$ with $5\nmid k$, $k<10$: $20$ values, so $400$ equally likely pairs.

Let $x=\cos a\pi$, $y=\sin b\pi$. The imaginary part of $(x+iy)^4$ is $4x^3y-4xy^3=4xy(x-y)(x+y)$, which is $0$ iff $x=0$, $y=0$ or $|x|=|y|$.

- $x=0$: $a\in\{\frac12,\frac32\}$, any $b$: $40$ pairs.
- $y=0$, $x\ne0$: $b\in\{0,1\}$, $a$ one of the other $18$ values: $36$ pairs.
- $|x|=|y|\ne0$: the common value must be $1$ or $\frac{\sqrt2}2$. (Values like $|\cos\frac\pi3|=\frac12$ would need $b=\frac16$, and $|\cos\frac{k\pi}5|$ would need a $b$ with denominator $10$; neither is allowed.) Value $1$: $a\in\{0,1\}$, $b\in\{\frac12,\frac32\}$: $4$ pairs. Value $\frac{\sqrt2}2$: $a,b\in\{\frac14,\frac34,\frac54,\frac74\}$: $16$ pairs.

Total $40+36+4+16=96$, probability $\frac{96}{400}=\frac6{25}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac6{25}$**

amc12-2015-12a-24.title: Count by the value of b
amc12-2015-12a-24.body:
Write $z=x+iy$; $z^4$ is real iff $z=0$ or $\arg z$ is a multiple of $45^\circ$, i.e. $z$ lies on the axes or on the lines $y=\pm x$.

- $b\in\{0,1\}$ ($y=0$): every $a$ works: $2\cdot20=40$.
- $b\in\{\frac12,\frac32\}$ ($y=\pm1$): need $x=0$ or $|x|=1$: $a\in\{0,1,\frac12,\frac32\}$: $2\cdot4=8$.
- $b\in\{\frac14,\frac34,\frac54,\frac74\}$ ($|y|=\frac{\sqrt2}2$): need $x=0$ or $|x|=\frac{\sqrt2}2$: $a\in\{\frac12,\frac32,\frac14,\frac34,\frac54,\frac74\}$: $4\cdot6=24$.
- Other $b$ (12 values with $y\neq0$, $|y|\neq1,\frac{\sqrt2}2$): $|x|=|y|$ never happens with an allowed $a$ (e.g. $|\sin\frac\pi3|=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ would need $a=\frac16$), so only $x=0$: $12\cdot2=24$.

Total $40+8+24+24=96$, probability $\frac{96}{400}=\frac6{25}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac6{25}$**

amc12-2015-12a-25.title: Key lemma: reciprocal square roots add
amc12-2015-12a-25.body:
**Lemma.** If circles of radii $r_1,r_2$ are tangent to a line and to each other, then the circle tangent to both and to the line, nestled between them, has radius $r$ with $\frac1{\sqrt r}=\frac1{\sqrt{r_1}}+\frac1{\sqrt{r_2}}$.

*Proof.* Two tangent circles of radii $p,q$ resting on a line touch it at points $2\sqrt{pq}$ apart (the centres are $p+q$ apart and differ in height by $|p-q|$, so the horizontal distance is $\sqrt{(p+q)^2-(p-q)^2}$). The horizontal distances add: $2\sqrt{r_1r_2}=2\sqrt{r_1r}+2\sqrt{r_2r}$; divide by $2\sqrt{r_1r_2r}$. ∎

Consecutive circles in the ordering are always tangent to each other (each new circle touches both of its neighbours), so the lemma applies at every stage. Let $w(C)=\frac1{\sqrt{r(C)}}$; each new circle's $w$ is the sum of its two neighbours' $w$. Let $s_k$ be the total $w$ over all circles in layers $0..k$, listed in order. When a new layer is added, each consecutive pair contributes the sum of the pair; every circle except the two outer ones is in two pairs, so the new layer adds $2s_{k-1}-w_0$ where $w_0=\frac1{70}+\frac1{73}$ is the sum for the two outermost (layer 0) circles. Hence $s_k=3s_{k-1}-w_0$, with $s_0=w_0$.

$s_1=2w_0$, $s_2=5w_0$, $s_3=14w_0$, $s_4=41w_0$, $s_5=122w_0$, $s_6=365w_0$.

$365\left(\frac1{70}+\frac1{73}\right)=365\cdot\frac{143}{5110}=\frac{143}{14}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{143}{14}$**

amc12-2015-12a-25.title: Closed form for the recursion
amc12-2015-12a-25.body:
With the lemma, $s_k-\frac{w_0}2=3\left(s_{k-1}-\frac{w_0}2\right)$, so $s_k=\frac{w_0}2\left(3^k+1\right)$. For $k=6$: $s_6=\frac{730}{2}w_0=365w_0$. Since $365=5\cdot73$ and $\frac1{70}+\frac1{73}=\frac{143}{70\cdot73}$, we get $s_6=\frac{5\cdot143}{70}=\frac{143}{14}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{143}{14}$**
